===Etymology 1===
{{root|en|ine-pro|*h₂eyḱ-}}
From {{der|en|enm|oun}}, {{m|enm|owen}}, from {{der|en|ang|āgen|t=own, proper, peculiar}}, originally the past participle of {{m|ang|āgan}}; from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*aigan|t=own}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*aiganaz|t=own}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₂eyḱ-|t=to have, possess}}. {{dbt|en|eigen-}}.
{{col-top|2|cog}}
Cognate with {{cog|sco|ain}}, {{m|sco|awin}}, {{m|sco|awn}}, {{m|sco|ayn|t=own}}, {{cog|stq|oain|t=own}}, {{cog|fy,nl,de|eigen|t=own}}, {{cog|da,nb,sv|egen|t=own}}, {{cog|fo|egin|t=own}}, {{cog|is|eigin}}, {{m|is|eiginn|t=own}}, {{cog|nn|eigen|t=own}}; also {{cog|os|исын|t=to take}}, {{cog|xto,txb|aik-|t=to know, recognize}}, {{cog|sa|ईश|t=owning, possessing}}. Originally past participle of the verb at hand in {{m+|en|owe}}.
{{col-bottom}}

====Alternative forms====
* {{alter|en|ain||Scotland}}
* {{alter|en|owne||obsolete}}

====Adjective====
{{en-adj|-}}

# {{senseid|en|belonging to}} [[belong|Belonging]] to; [[possess]]ed; [[acquire]]d and [[designate]]d by; [[proper]] to; [[property]] of; [[title]]d to; [[held]] in one's [[name]]; [[under]]/[[using]] the name of. {{n-g|Often marks a possessive determiner as reflexive, referring back to the subject of the clause or sentence.}}
#* {{RQ:King James Version|Deuteronomy|24|16|passage=The fathers shall not bee put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: euery man shall be put to death for his '''owne''' sinne.}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Tempest|IV|i|page=14|passage={{smallcaps|Prospero}}: Fairely ſpoke ; / Sit then, and talke with her, ſhe is thine '''owne''' ;}}
#* {{RQ:Churchill Celebrity|chapter=8|passage=I corralled the judge, and we started off across the fields, in no very mild state of fear of that gentleman's wife, whose vigilance was seldom relaxed. And thus we came by a circuitous route to Mohair, the judge occupied by his '''own''' guilty thoughts, and I by others not less disturbing.}}
#* {{RQ:Maxwell Mirror and the Lamp|chapter=10|passage=He looked round the poor room, at the distempered walls, and the bad engravings in meretricious frames, the crinkly paper and wax flowers on the chiffonier; and he thought of a room like Father Bryan's, with panelling, with cut glass, with tulips in silver pots, such a room as he had hoped to have for his '''own'''.}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|date=2013-06-21|author=w:Oliver Burkeman
|volume=189|issue=2|page=27|magazine=w:The Guardian Weekly
|title=[http://www.guardian.co.uk/technology/2013/may/10/conscious-computing-twitter-facebook-google The tao of tech]
|passage=The dirty secret of the internet is that all this distraction and interruption is immensely profitable. Web companies like to boast about […], or offering services that let you{{...}} "share the things you love with the world" and so on. But the real way to build a successful online business is to be better than your rivals at undermining people's control of their '''own''' attention.}}
# Not [[share|shared]].
#: {{ux|en|When we move into the new house, the kids will each have their '''own''' bedroom.}}
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} [[peculiar|Peculiar]], [[domestic]].
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} Not [[foreign]].

=====Usage notes=====
* Often used for implication of ownership, often with emphasis. In modern usage, it always follows a possessive determiner, or a noun in the possessive case.

===Etymology 2===
{{wp}}
{{root|en|ine-pro|*h₂eyḱ-}}
A {{back-formation|en|owner|nocap=1}}. Compare {{cog|ang|āgnian}}, {{cog|nl|eigenen}}, {{cog|de|eignen}}, {{cog|sv|ägna}}.

====Verb====
{{en-verb}}

# {{senseid|en|owner}}{{lb|en|transitive}} To have [[rightful]] [[possession]] of ([[property]], [[goods]] or [[capital]]); to have [[legal]] [[title]] to; to acquire a [[property]] or [[asset]].
#: {{ux|en|I '''own''' this car.}}
# {{senseid|en|sovereignty}}{{lb|en|transitive}} To have recognized political sovereignty over a place, territory, as distinct from the ordinary connotation of property ownership.
#: {{ux|en|The United States '''owns''' Point Roberts by the terms of the Treaty of Oregon.}}
# {{senseid|en|overwhelm}}{{lb|en|transitive|informal}} To defeat or [[embarrass]]; to [[overwhelm]].
#: {{ux|en|I will '''own''' my enemies.}}
#: {{ux|en|If he wins, he will '''own''' you.}}
# {{senseid|en|enslave}}{{lb|en|transitive}} To virtually or figuratively [[enslave]].
# {{senseid|en|gaming}}{{lb|en|online gaming|slang}} To defeat, dominate, or be above.
#: {{syn|en|pwn}}
# {{senseid|en|pwned}}{{lb|en|transitive|computing|slang}} To [[illicit]]ly obtain [[administrator|administrative]] access to a [[computer system]], thereby having full access to all the [[file]]s thereon (including [[executable#Noun|executables]]).
#: {{syn|en|pwn|0wn}}
#* {{quote-newsgroup
|en
|title=Re: An unusual situation
|accessdate=2016-09-24
|author=The Happiest Dragon Alive!!
|passage="TH15 5Y5T3M 15 '''0WN3D'''"
|url=https://groups.google.com/forum/#!original/alt.sysadmin.recovery/IsdIZqfW_sM/9UTRiIoSy74J
|date=1996/06/21
|id=4qe8pc$8ti@nerd.apk.net
}}
# {{senseid|en|excel}}{{lb|en|intransitive|slang}} To be very good.
# {{senseid|en|admit}}{{lb|en|intransitive}} To [[admit]], [[concede]], [[grant]], [[allow]]; not to deny.
#* {{RQ:Melville Moby-Dick|passage=I '''own''' thy speechless, placeless power; but to the last gasp of my earthquake life will dispute its unconditional, unintegral mastery in me.}}
#* {{RQ:Conrad Heart of Darkness|part=I|passage=I am sorry to '''own''' I began to worry then.}}
#* {{RQ:Lawrence Sons and Lovers|passage=They learned how perfectly peaceful the home could be. And they almost regretted—though none of them would have '''owned''' to such callousness—that their father was soon coming back.|5}}
# {{senseid|en|acknowledge}}{{lb|en|transitive}} To [[acknowledge]].
#: {{ux|en|I must '''own''' that I have been at fault all this time.}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Tempest|v|text=Two of those fellows you must know and '''own'''.}}
#* {{RQ:Carlyle Past and Present|2|1, ''Jocelin of Brakelond''|text=It must be '''owned''', the good Jocelin, spite of his beautiful childlike character, is but an altogether imperfect 'mirror' of these old-world things!}}
# {{senseid|en|proudly acknowledge}}{{lb|en|transitive}} To [[proud]]ly [[acknowledge]]; to not be [[ashamed]] or [[embarrassed]] of.
# {{senseid|en|own up}}{{lb|en|transitive}} To take [[responsibility]] for.
#* {{RQ:NYT|en|title=As Political Violence Rises, Trump Condemns One Side|date=2025-09-11|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/11/us/politics/political-violence-trump-blame.html|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20251031213905/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/11/us/politics/political-violence-trump-blame.html|author=Luke Broadwater; Alan Feuer|quotee=w:Nancy Mace|passage=Representative Nancy Mace, Republican of South Carolina, told reporters that Democrats “'''own'''” the assassination of Mr. Kirk. When a reporter questioned her about attacks on Democrats, she cut him off. “Democrats '''own''' this,” she said. “We’re talking about Charlie Kirk right now.”}}
# {{senseid|en|recognise}}{{lb|en|transitive}} To [[recognise]].
#: {{ux|en|I '''own''' him as a son of my own.}}
# {{senseid|en|claim}}{{lb|en|transitive}} To [[claim]] as one's own.
# {{senseid|en|confess}}{{lb|en|intransitive|UK|_|dialectal}} To [[confess]].

==English==
{{wp}}

===Alternative forms===
* {{alt|en|traffick|qq1=archaic|traffique|qq2=obsolete}}

===Etymology===
From {{bor|en|frm|trafique}}, {{m|frm|traffique||traffic}}, from {{der|en|it|traffico||traffic}} from {{m|it|trafficare||to carry on trade}}. Potentially from {{der|en|la-vul|*trānsfrīcāre||to rub across}}; Klein instead suggests the Italian has ultimate origin in {{der|en|ar|تَفْرِيق||distribution, dispersion}}, reshaped to match the native prefix {{m|it|tra-||trans-}}.
{{root|en|ar|ف ر ق}}<!--possibly--> Displaced native {{noncog|ang|mangung||traffic, trade, commerce}}.

The adjectival sense is possibly influenced by {{der|en|tl|trapik}} and follows a general trend in Philippine English to construct a noun from an adjective.<ref>{{R:OED Online|entry=traffic|pos=adj|id=33840333|date=December 2021}}</ref>

===Pronunciation===
* {{enPR|trăf'ĭk}}, {{IPA|en|/ˈtɹæfɪk/|a=RP,GA}}
* {{audio|en|En-us-traffic.ogg|a=GA}}
* {{rhymes|en|æfɪk|s=2}}
* {{hyphenation|en|traf|fic}}

===Noun===
{{en-noun|-|s}}

# {{senseid|en|movement}} Moving [[pedestrian]]s or [[vehicle]]s, or the [[flux]] or [[passage]] thereof.
#: {{syn|en|[[travel]] (U.S.)}}
#: {{ux|en|The '''traffic''' is slow during [[rush hour]].}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Romeo and Juliet Q1-2|chapter=Prologue|passage=VVhoſe miſaduentures, piteous ouerthrovves, / (Through the continuing of their Fathers ſtrife, / And death-markt paſſage of their Parents rage) / Is novv the tvvo hovvres '''traffique''' of our Stage.}}
# {{senseid|en|commercial}} The [[commercial]] [[transportation]] or [[exchange]] of [[goods]], or the movement of [[passenger]]s or people.
#* {{RQ:Defoe Crusoe|passage=I had three large axes, and abundance of hatchets (for we carried the hatchets for '''traffic''' with the Indians).}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=2007|author=John Darwin|title=After Tamerlane|publisher=Penguin|page=12
|passage=Its units of study are regions or oceans, long-distance trades [...], the '''traffic''' of cults and beliefs between cultures and continents.}}

#: {{syn|en|trafficking<q:more common>}}
#* {{RQ:Guardian|author=Alfred W. McCoy|title=How the heroin trade explains the US-UK failure in Afghanistan|date=2018-01-09|url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2018/jan/09/how-the-heroin-trade-explains-the-us-uk-failure-in-afghanistan|passage=They, in turn, had long dominated the drug '''traffic''' in the area of north-east Afghanistan that they controlled during the Taliban years.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20261022095104/https://www.theguardian.com/news/2018/jan/09/how-the-heroin-trade-explains-the-us-uk-failure-in-afghanistan|archivedate=22 October 2026}}

|passage=The parish stank of idolatry, abominable rites were practiced in secret, and in all the bounds there was no one had a more evil name for the black '''traffic''' than one Alison Sempill, who bode at the Skerburnfoot.}}
#* {{RQ:Guardian|author=Charles Arthur|title=Porn sites get more internet traffic in UK than social networks or shopping|date=2013-07-26|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2013/jul/26/porn-sites-internet-traffic-uk|passage=Internet '''traffic''' to legal pornography sites in the UK comprised 8.5% of all "clicks" on web pages in June – exceeding those for shopping, news, business or social networks, according to new data obtained exclusively by the Guardian.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20261016230022/https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2013/jul/26/porn-sites-internet-traffic-uk|archivedate=16 October 2026}}

====Usage notes====
* ''Video'' is used in contrast with {{m|en|audio}}, which is sound only. It is also sometimes used in contrast with {{m|en|film}} to describe all other motion picture formats, such as [[videotape]] and [[digital video]]. The words ''video'' and {{m|en|movie}} have some synonymous overlap, but a feature film on the big screen is only a ''movie'' in {{l|en|idiom|idiomatic}} use (not a ''video''), and web-era user-created videos are usually not called ''movies'' except in certain contexts.
* The plural {{m|en|videmus}} is rare and used for humorous effect. It is the first-person plural form of the Latin verb ("we see") in the same way that {{m|la|videō}} is the singular.

===Etymology===
{{root|en|ine-pro|*lewbʰ- (cut off)}}
From {{inh|en|enm|librarie}}, from {{der|en|xno|librarie}}, from {{der|en|fro|librairie}}, from {{der|en|la|librarium||bookcase, chest for books}}, from {{m|la|librarius||concerning books}}, from {{m|la|liber||the inner bark of trees; paper, parchment, book}}, probably derived from a {{der|en|ine-pro|-}} base {{m|ine-pro|*lewbʰ-|*leub(ʰ)-|to strip, to peel}}. Displaced native {{ncog|enm|bochous|bochous, bokhus|lit=book house}}, from {{ncog|ang|bōchūs}} (compare {{m|en|bookhouse}}).

{{cog|roa|-}} cognates often mean “bookshop” instead: {{cog|fr|librairie}}, {{cog|it|libreria}}, {{cog|es|librería}}, {{cog|ro|librărie}} and {{cog|pt|livraria}}. This is a relatively recent innovation (16th century in French), which ended up displacing the earlier sense.

===Etymology===
The original sense ([[can]]ned [[ham]]) is a proprietary name registered by Geo. A. Hormel & Co. in U.S., 1937. It is presumed to be a conflation of either "'''sp'''iced h'''am'''" or "'''s'''houlder of '''p'''ork and h'''am'''"<ref>{{cite-web |title=What does the SPAM brand name mean? |work=SPAM |accessdate=6 July 2013 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131014172553/http://www.spam.com/spam-101/what-does-the-spam-brand-name-mean |archivedate=14 October 2013 }}</ref> but was soon extended to other kinds of canned meat. Hormel spells the trademarked name in all upper case.

The use for unsolicited and unwanted email derives from a {{w|Monty Python's Flying Circus}} sketch.<ref>{{cite-av|en|episode=Spam|date=1970-12-15|number=12|season=2|title=w:Monty Python's Flying Circus|mainauthor=w:Monty Python|writer=Michael Palin;Terry Jones|network=BBC One|publisher=BBC|location=London|url=http://us.imdb.com/title/tt0650991}}</ref> In the 1970 sketch, a group of Vikings in a restaurant repeatedly chant the word "spam". The earliest recorded real-life use for this sense occurs around 1993 which finds reference in a newsgroup post dated March 31, 1993, but the term may have been in use on "[[multi-user dungeon|Multi-User Dungeons]]" ([[MUD]]s) in the 1980s.<ref>{{cite-web|en|title=Origin of the term "spam" to mean net abuse|author=Brad Templeton|work=Brad Templeton's Home Page|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120716231643/http://www.templetons.com/brad/spamterm.html|accessdate=2025-10-05}}</ref>

{{root|en|ine-pro|*stel-}}

The {{l|en|local|id=ring|ring-theoretic senses}} derive from {{w|Wolfgang Krull|Krull}}, who first referred to Noetherian commutative rings with a unique maximal ideal as "Stellenring" ({{compound|de|Stellen|ring|t1=place|nocat=1}}) in 1938.<ref>Krull, Wolfgang. "Dimensionstheorie in Stellenringen [47]". Volume 1+2, edited by Paulo Ribenboim, Berlin, Boston: De Gruyter, 1999, pp. 730-734. https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110801026.730</ref> The term was inspired by [[algebraic geometry]], where local rings encode information about the behavior of curves (surfaces, etc.) at points; hence, describe "local" behavior.
